title: API Inspector Training in the Southeast: Terminals and Mills
description: API 510, 570, 580 and 653 exam prep for Florida, Georgia, Carolinas and Tennessee: fuel terminals, pipelines, pulp mills and chemical plants. Studied online.
h1: API inspector training for the Southeast: fuel terminals, pipelines, pulp mills and chemical plants
html:
Ask where API inspectors work and most people point at the Gulf Coast refineries. The Southeast is a different market. Apart from Valero's refinery in Memphis, the region's API work does not revolve around crude refining; it sits in the fuel terminals that receive products by ship and pipeline, in the pipelines themselves, in pulp and paper mills, in chemical plants and in power stations. That changes which certification pays off, and in some jobs it means an API certificate is useful knowledge rather than a requirement. This page is for inspectors, technicians and engineers in Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Tennessee and southern Virginia. It explains honestly where API 510, API 570, API 580 and API 653 fit in the regional economy and how to prepare for the exam with Atlantis's self-paced online course.

Florida: fuel arrives by water, and API 653 is written into state rules

Florida is not connected to the Gulf Coast refineries by pipeline, so the U.S. Energy Information Administration has described almost all of its gasoline as arriving by ship and barge at ports including Tampa, Port Everglades, Port Canaveral and Jacksonville, then moving out of terminal tanks by truck. Two port examples show the scale of the tank work that follows:

  • Port Everglades says companies at the port store and distribute one-third of Florida's energy requirements, with seventeen petroleum terminal and pipeline firms operating inside port jurisdiction, supplying twelve counties and five international airports.
  • Port Tampa Bay names petroleum as its largest commodity sector, at more than 17 million tons of oil, gasoline and jet fuel a year, much of it moving inland by pipeline. Its bulk facilities list includes Central Florida Pipeline, TransMontaigne and Buckeye Terminals, and EIA notes the Central Florida Pipeline system carries products from the Tampa Bay ports to Orlando.

What makes Florida distinctive for a candidate is the state rule for field-erected tanks. Florida Administrative Code rule 62-762.702 requires these tanks to be evaluated, and their re-testing frequency set and implemented, in accordance with API Standard 653, with the evaluation certified by a Florida-licensed professional engineer or approved by an API 653 certified inspector. Field-erected tanks under 250,000 gallons may use STI SP001 instead. In other words, Florida's tank regulation names the very certificate this course prepares you to sit for, which gives terminal inspectors there a clear reason to put API 653 first.

Pipelines and inland terminals across Georgia, the Carolinas and Tennessee

Inland, fuel moves by two long products pipelines. Colonial Pipeline describes a system of about 5,500 miles from Houston to Linden, New Jersey, with storage at Greensboro, North Carolina, for regional distribution. The Plantation pipeline, operated by Kinder Morgan and headquartered in Alpharetta, Georgia, runs about 3,100 miles from Baton Rouge towards Washington and serves Atlanta, Charlotte, Greensboro, Birmingham, Chattanooga, Knoxville, Greenville and Spartanburg, Roanoke and Richmond. EIA adds that Florida's panhandle is supplied from a terminal at Bainbridge, Georgia, on a spur of the Colonial system.

Every delivery point on those lines means breakout and products tanks, manifolds, pumps and transfer piping. Federal pipeline rules at 49 CFR 195.432 require in-service atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks to be inspected according to API 653, without its risk-based alternative for the internal interval, and terminal piping is commonly inspected using API 570 methods. For a Southeast candidate who works on these systems, API 653 and API 570 are usually the right pair.

Which certification fits which Southeast employer

Employer typeTypical equipmentCertification that usually fits
Port and pipeline fuel terminalsFloating-roof and fixed-roof products tanks, dock and transfer pipingAPI 653 first, API 570 second
Valero's Memphis refinery on Lake McKellar, about 180,000 barrels per calendar day of crude capacity in EIA's 2026 surveyRefinery process vessels, unit piping, tank fieldsAPI 510 and API 570, with API 653 for the tank field
Chemical plants, such as Eastman's Kingsport site, which Eastman calls one of the largest integrated chemical manufacturing sites in North AmericaReactors, columns, exchangers, alloy pipingAPI 510 and API 570, with API 580 for programme roles
Pulp and paper millsDigesters, liquor and chemical-recovery vessels, process pipingAPI 510 knowledge alongside TAPPI inspection guidance and the mill's own programme
LNG, such as the Elba Island terminal near SavannahProcess vessels and piping around liquefaction unitsAPI 510 and API 570; refrigerated LNG tanks are built to other standards
Power stationsBoilers, deaerators, heaters, fuel oil tanksState boiler and pressure vessel rules first; API 653 for fuel oil tankage

Valero's fact sheet places the Memphis refinery on 250 acres beside Lake McKellar, off the Mississippi, and says nearly all of its output is light products such as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. For an API candidate around Memphis, its vessel, piping and tank programmes are the closest thing the Southeast offers to Gulf Coast refinery inspection work.

Elba Island, about five miles downstream from Savannah, began as an LNG import and storage terminal and now has ten liquefaction units added in a project that Kinder Morgan completed in 2020. Power stations deserve a plain warning: the boilers and many of the vessels there are inspected under state law and the National Board Inspection Code, so an inspector who works mostly in power generation should check what their employer and jurisdiction actually ask for before investing in an API certificate.

Pulp and paper: where API 510 meets TAPPI guidance

The Georgia Forestry Association counted eleven pulp mills in Georgia in 2024, with pulp and paper making up 38 percent of the state's direct forest-industry jobs. The sector is changing too: International Paper closed its Savannah and Riceboro mills and Georgia-Pacific closed its Cedar Springs mill in 2025. The mills that remain across Georgia, Florida and the Carolinas still run large pressure vessels and long runs of process piping, and they still need people who can inspect them.

API 510 states that it applies to refining and chemical process vessels, and it was developed by that industry for its own needs. Whether a mill applies it depends on the owner and the jurisdiction. In practice many mill inspection programmes borrow its methods for corrosion rates, remaining life and intervals, and add industry guidance for equipment the API codes do not describe. The best-known example is the digester: TAPPI's TIP 0402-27 gives guidelines for inspecting continuous digesters and impregnation vessels, and TIP 0402-22 covers batch digesters. A mill inspector who knows API 510 well and reads the TAPPI papers for their equipment is a strong candidate for both mill and chemical-plant jobs.

Worked example: an API 510 internal inspection interval

A carbon steel vessel shell read 0.625 inch at one inspection and 0.580 inch at the next, five years later. Its required thickness at the design conditions is 0.500 inch. The corrosion rate is 0.045 divided by 5, or 0.009 inch a year. The remaining life is the corrosion allowance left, 0.080 inch, divided by 0.009, which is about 8.9 years. Unless an RBI assessment justifies something else, API 510 limits the period between internal or on-stream inspections to half the remaining life or ten years, whichever is less, so this vessel's interval is about 4.4 years. Had the remaining life been under four years, API 510's separate rule for short remaining lives would apply instead. Expect the exam to test both the arithmetic and which rule governs.

Heat, humidity and storm season: what Southeast work demands

The Southeast climate shapes the damage an inspector sees. Warm, wet air and coastal salt drive external corrosion on tank shells, structural steel and dock piping. Insulated lines that run warm but not hot sit in the temperature band where corrosion under insulation develops, roughly 10°F to 350°F for carbon steel, and insulation that never fully dries out makes it worse. Terminal piping that passes from soil into air needs attention at that interface, and tank bottoms depend on cathodic protection and linings, the subjects of API RP 651 and API RP 652 that appear in the API 653 Body of Knowledge.

Storm season adds a scheduling problem. Owners plan tank out-of-service work, repairs and painting around it, and inspectors are often pulled into preparation and recovery work. When you choose an exam window, leave room for that.

Preparing for an API exam from a Southeast job

The course is built for people who cannot attend scheduled classes: terminal inspectors on rotating shifts, mill inspectors working outages and contractors travelling across several states. You enrol, study the code material and practice papers at your own pace, and send questions to an instructor whenever a clause or calculation needs explaining. A few points apply particularly in this region:

  • Florida terminal candidates should spend real time on API 650 as well as API 653. API's effectivity sheet for the 2027 API 653 windows lists API 650's 14th edition and API 653's 5th edition with its addenda, alongside RP 575, RP 651, RP 652 and parts of ASME Sections V and IX, and repair questions often send you back to the construction standard.
  • Mill and chemical-plant candidates aiming at API 510 should practise the Section VIII calculations for shells and heads under internal pressure until they are routine, because minimum-thickness and rerating questions are built on them.
  • Book the test-centre seat early. Prometric lists test centres in and around the Southeast's larger cities, and seats within a window go first-come, first-served. API 580 can be taken by remote proctoring, according to API's scheduling page.

Eligibility for Southeast candidates

API administers the examinations and issues certification, and it sets the eligibility rules. For API 510, API 570 and API 653 it counts experience gained in the last ten years while employed by or under contract to an authorized inspection agency: one year for an engineering or technology degree, two years for a two-year degree or certificate, three years for a high-school diploma and five or more years without formal education, with at least one year of supervising or performing inspection in the longer routes. For API 653 the rules are set out in Annex D of the standard. Southeast routes include terminal technicians moving into inspection roles, NDT technicians at contract inspection companies, mill maintenance staff joining an inspection group, and engineers at chemical plants. The full rules are on the API 653, API 510 and API 570 certification pages.

For employers in the Southeast

Terminal companies, pipeline operators and mill owners can sponsor one candidate or several, and fees are quoted on request for the group. Because no one has to travel to a classroom, an employer with sites in Tampa, Jacksonville and Atlanta can enrol inspectors at each site at the same time. Each candidate applies to API on their own and sits the exam on their own. For NDT training in the region, see Atlantis's pages for Jacksonville, Tampa, Savannah, Atlanta, Charlotte, Memphis and Norfolk; for AWS CWI exam prep, see Jacksonville, Tampa and Atlanta.

faq.q: Is API 653 worth getting if I inspect tanks in Florida?
faq.a: For field-erected tank work it is directly relevant. Florida's rule 62-762.702 requires field-erected tanks to be evaluated, and their re-testing frequency set, in accordance with API 653, with the evaluation certified by a Florida-licensed professional engineer or approved by an API 653 certified inspector. Tanks under 250,000 gallons may follow STI SP001 instead.

faq.q: I work at a paper mill. Will API 510 help me?
faq.a: Often, yes. API 510 is written for refining and chemical process vessels, but its methods for corrosion rates, remaining life, intervals, repairs and rerating are widely borrowed by mill inspection programmes, which add TAPPI guidance for digesters and other mill equipment. Whether API 510 formally applies at your mill depends on the owner and the jurisdiction, so ask your inspection lead how the programme is written.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Atlanta, Jacksonville or Charlotte?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Atlanta, Jacksonville, Charlotte or any other Southeast city; Atlantis's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad. The API exam-prep courses are studied online at your own pace, with an instructor answering questions, and API runs the examinations at Prometric test centres.

faq.q: Can I take the API 580 exam remotely?
faq.a: API's exam scheduling page lists API 580 among the examinations that can be taken through Prometric's ProProctor remote platform. API 510, API 570 and API 653 are not available remotely and must be taken at a test centre. API sets the delivery options, so confirm them for your window when you apply.

faq.q: Do LNG storage tanks at a site like Elba Island fall under API 653?
faq.a: API 653 is written for atmospheric storage tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor, API 12C. Refrigerated LNG tanks are built to other standards, so API 653 is not their core document. The process vessels and piping around an LNG plant are a much better fit for API 510 and API 570.

faq.q: How should storm season affect when I sit the exam?
faq.a: Choose an exam window that does not collide with the months when your site is most likely to be preparing for or recovering from storms, or with a planned outage. API runs each examination in set windows with application deadlines, and a missed window means a new application. Current windows are on the API exam schedule page.

faq.q: I inspect power plant equipment. Do I need an API certificate?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Power station boilers and many of their vessels are inspected under state boiler and pressure vessel law and the National Board Inspection Code, and the inspectors who sign for the jurisdiction hold commissions rather than API certificates. API 653 can still be valuable if you look after fuel oil tankage, and API 510 knowledge transfers well. Check what your employer requires first.

faq.q: Can our terminal company enrol inspectors at several Southeast sites?
faq.a: Yes. Send one enquiry with the number of candidates at each site and the code each one is preparing for, and the quote covers the whole group. Each inspector studies at their own pace with instructor support, applies to API individually and sits the examination individually.
